cells.tense: Here, with the pen, you are meeting the ending as it happens.
cells.act: tend the fire without burning out
cells.ask: Choose the thing this ending keeps pulling you back to. Tend it on purpose — a few minutes, a few times a day. When it starts asking for more than that, put it down for the day.
cells.core:
You're in a room where something is being cleared away, and you're meeting it with your eyes open. Most people brace here — they treat the ending as a loss to survive. You're doing it differently. You're still curious about what's underneath, what this opens up, what the feeling is actually made of. That fresh way in is why this ending can finish cleanly instead of dragging.

What's steady in you is this: you can keep a small fire going without letting it eat everything around it. That's what this stretch needs. Choose one thing the ending keeps tugging at — an object, a room, a small routine tied to what's ending — and tend it on purpose. A few minutes daily. When it starts to ask for more, put it down for the day. That's the whole instruction. What you'll have is a clearing done by your own hand, at a pace your body can carry.
cells.sheetLine: You can meet this ending without making it a battle.
cells.verb: Meeting what ends with fresh feeling, before knowing what it will become
cells.place: In the clearing where a necessary ending is being allowed to finish

cells.tense: You are already living past the ending, before it has finished happening.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: Keep one small living thing going — water, light, soil, whatever it turns out to want. Let what it needs teach you slowly.
cells.core:
You've jumped the ending. In your head the room is already cleared, the new thing already arranged, the feeling already resolved, and you're standing in that future trying to make the present match it. It's a way of skipping the slow part. The trouble is the ending won't be skipped. It's still happening, underneath your plans, and it's getting less attention than it needs.

Something slower is available. Find one small living thing — a plant, a pot on a windowsill, a cutting in a glass — and keep it going. Water it, move it toward light, watch what changes. The point isn't the plant. It's learning what something needs by observing it, not by deciding what it should need. That's the same skill this clearing is asking for. What you'll have is a hand that knows how to wait for what's actually there.

cells.tense: You keep walking toward a door you already stepped through.
cells.act: follow a raw curiosity with no use for it
cells.ask: Some afternoon, follow whatever catches your attention for five minutes — a sound, a question, something you keep half-noticing. Make nothing of it, and stop when you're done.
cells.core:
The ending seems to have passed already. Not all of it, but the part you keep acting like is still ahead of you. The news hasn't landed. You're reaching for a handle that isn't there anymore, and the room around you is the one on the other side.

What refills this is smaller than the ending. Some afternoon, follow whatever catches you — a sound, a question, something you keep coming back to — for five minutes, with nothing to show for it and no point to make. That kind of wondering doesn't need to know where it's going. You just look at one thing closely because it's there. What you'll have is a small pull, and you can rest.

cells.tense: You are clearing this ground already, and calling it something else.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Sit down and put the plain facts on one page — what is, what changed, what remains. No feeling words. Then close the notebook.
cells.core:
You've been doing the clearing. Not as a project, not as a decision — as the thing you're quietly getting on with. Someone asks how you are and you say fine, busy. Meanwhile the endings keep finishing through your hands, one after another, and you've been calling it ordinary. It isn't. What's happening here is your work, and your account of it leaves that out.

There's an older form of this in you, and it's simpler than the story. Sit down and put the plain facts on one page: what is, what changed, what remains. No feeling words. Not to work anything out — just to see the record in your own hand. Then close the notebook. What you'll have is your name on what you've been doing. The clearing was yours, and the page says so.
